mainEntity.name: How much difference do monthly contributions make?

acceptedAnswer.text: A great deal over long periods — consistent contributions often account for more of the final balance than the initial investment itself, thanks to compounding.

mainEntity.name: Should I invest a lump sum or spread it out (dollar-cost averaging)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Historically, investing a lump sum immediately outperforms spreading it out on average, since markets trend upward over time — but dollar-cost averaging can reduce regret risk and smooth out volatility for some investors.

mainEntity.name: What's a reasonable fee to pay on investments?

acceptedAnswer.text: Low-cost index funds often charge well under 0.5% annually, while some actively managed funds charge 1% or more — fees compound over time just like returns, so lower costs meaningfully help long-term growth.

Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of market price, which smooths out the effect of market timing and is the strategy this calculator's monthly contribution feature effectively models.

mainEntity.name: Should I use a tax-advantaged account for long-term investing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Accounts like a 401(k), IRA, or Roth IRA offer tax benefits that can meaningfully improve long-term after-tax growth compared to a standard taxable brokerage account, making them worth prioritizing for retirement-focused investing.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate return on investment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Subtract the starting value from the ending value and divide by the starting value. For example, $10,000 growing to $22,000 is an ROI of 120%. ROI ignores time, so use CAGR to compare investments held for different periods.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between ROI and CAGR?

acceptedAnswer.text: ROI is the total percentage gain over the whole holding period. CAGR converts that gain into the steady yearly rate that would produce it, using (ending ÷ starting)^(1 ÷ years) − 1. $10,000 growing to $22,000 over 8 years is a 120% ROI and a CAGR of about 10.36%.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate real return after inflation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide one plus your nominal return by one plus the inflation rate, then subtract one. An 8% return with 3% inflation is a real return of about 4.85% a year.

mainEntity.name: How do fees affect investment growth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fees come out of your return every year, so they compound. In this calculator, $10,000 plus $300 a month for 20 years ends at about $225,974 at 8% but $196,665 at 7%, so a 1 percentage point fee costs roughly $29,300.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to double my money?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Rule of 72 estimates it as 72 divided by your annual return. At 8%, money doubles in about 9 years (the exact figure is 9.01 years). Regular contributions shorten the time to double your total balance.
